newsitem.title: USA: IMF, donors set to help Thailand overcome crisis.
newsitem.headline: IMF, donors set to help Thailand overcome crisis.

text.p: A donor meeting in Tokyo on Monday will discuss an aid package of up to $15 billion as countries and international financial institutions seek to help tiger-economy Thailand back onto its financial feet.

A deal, underpinned by financial reforms drawn up by the International Monetary Fund, would produce the biggest loan package for a single country since the international community offered almost $40 billion to bail out Mexico in 1995.

Monetary sources in Washington and Tokyo say Japan's Export-Import Bank is likely to be the single biggest donor, followed by the IMF, other financial institutions and other states in the Asia-Pacific region.
Thailand is looking for $12-15 billion to plug financial holes created when it floated the baht currency last mohth.
Bangkok turned reluctantly to the IMF for help last week after other donors made clear that an IMF economic programme was an essential element of a loan package.
"We are very pleased that Thailand has taken this step," U.S. Undersecretary of State Stuart Eizenstat told Reuters Financial Television on Friday.
"We support the IMF programme. We think that focusing on correcting some of the fundamental problems that the Thai economy has is the best way to stabilise the baht."
Asked if he thought a deal was imminent, he replied: "I think there is a good chance."

Thailand, long one of the booming "tiger-economies" of Southeast Asia, has already introduced an austerity package to meet IMF demands, raising value added tax, announcing plans to cut the current account deficit and closing more than half the country's financial institutions.
The baht traded at 30.90 to the dollar in offshore markets on Friday, down some 27 percent from its pre-float levels of 24.25 to the dollar as dealers waited for Monday's talks.
An IMF mission has been assessing the situation in Thailand and officials will report their conclusions both to the Tokyo donor meeting and to headquarters in Washington.

"If the IMF experts can go to the meeting with a complete package they can seek the support of the IMF board and then look for support from the international community," said an international monetary source.
But another source said it was not clear when the package would be finalised because some donors might have to report back to governments or parliaments.
"We may not be at a decision point yet," the source said. "I do not know if all the countries will be in a position to make a firm commitment."
U.S. officials have made clear that Washington will not participate directly in a Thai bailout -- in stark contrast to the Mexico rescue plan, which was heavily U.S.-funded.
But they say the United States will back an IMF lending programme, provided it is supported by appropriate policies.

"We are obviously concerned with the economic and financial situation generally and that is why we have said we are prepared to support extraordinary (IMF) access for Thailand if and when an appropriate programme is agreed," Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Saturday.

"The crucial elements of such a programme are strong fiscal adjustment, measures to reform the financial system and remove capital controls and achieve greatly improved transparency in economic management."
Eizenstat said the United States would be involved in any package through the IMF, which is using rules drawn up after the Mexico crisis to speed the progress of a Thai rescue plan.
"The IMF has a special emergency package and in effect this already incorporates a U.S. contribution," he said.
"This kind of standby facility is going to prove increasingly useful for all (IMF) members who have this kind of crisis. It is a good fallback position."
